utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning the interpreters and the technicians. Are you ready? Good morning. Mr. Dubuisson, please introduce today's matter.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, today matter is IT-95-14/1-T. The Prosecutor versus Zlatko Aleksovski. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Would the Prosecution please introduce itself for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, my name is Mr. Niemann and I appear with my colleagues Mr. Meddegoda and Ms. Erasmus for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Mikulicic, please introduce yourself for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning Your Honours, my name is Goran Mikulicic and together with my colleague Mr. Joka I represent the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to continue then with today's case. Mr. Mikulicic you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence would like to call Dr. Zvonmir Stipac. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Do you hear me? Before you are seated, I would ask that you read the solemn declaration that is being shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please be seated. You are now going to respond to questions that will be put to you by Mr. Mikulicic, who is there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You are now appearing before this Tribunal as witness for Defence. As Defence counsel, I would like to put to you a couple of questions and I would kindly ask you to respond to the best of your recollection. Dr. Stipac, could you tell us your personal data, where and when were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Zvonmir Stipac and I was born in Zenica on the 8th of June, 1961.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, where did you go to school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I completed elementary school in Busovaca and I graduated from the school of medical faculty at Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where did you complete your secondary education?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background and what is your religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My ethnic background is Croatian and I am a Catholic, Roman Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, you said you completed elementary school in Busovaca and secondary school and grammar school in Vitez, where did you live at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Throughout that time I lived in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Since you were born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said you graduated from the faculty of medicine in Sarajevo, where were you employed after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I found a job at the health centre in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In what year was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1993. This is when I begin my internship, at the beginning of '93, in January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As a physician, do you have any specialisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am currently having my specialisation, I am specialising in gynaecology and obstetrics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, what kind of job did you have at the medical centre in Busovaca? Did you work for any particular department or did you provide services to patients in general?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which period do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you were initially employed and after that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So from the beginning of conflict I was, I worked mostly for the emergency department and I would most often be on night duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, the health centre in Busovaca is a medical institution which is responsible for which area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It covers the territory of the Municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How many people, approximately, use services at your medical centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, before the war it was roughly 20.000 and during the conflict somewhat less and then including refugees, perhaps 15.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how many physicians were there in the first half of 1993? That is how many were employed at the medical centre in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for the first half of the year 1993, I can tell you that there were very few physicians. Those who were employed did not actually work, some of them did not actually work, so there were may be two or three physicians in total. As for paramedical staff, I can't give you exact figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, what was the situation with the medical equipment in the first half of 1993 and prior to that in 1992, what was it at the medical centre in Busovaca, what kind of medical protection was your centre able to offer at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, it was mostly a medical institution for primary health care. We had one specialist, a gynaecologist, and that was all. We had an old x-ray machine, an old ECG machine and we had a laboratory, of course, but that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you have any wing where you could admit patients for treatment at the health centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not have such possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And when it was necessary for you to provide hospital treatment to a patient, what would you do? I am referring to the same time period, 1992, and the first half of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would refer patients to the Nova Bila hospital. It was a hospital that was located in a religious institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In a church?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So it was a makeshift medical institution, am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This all happened in the first half of 1993, but what was the situation in the second half of 1992, which hospital would you refer them to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would refer them to the regional hospital in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember in -- when was it that the last patient or last patients were referred to the medical centre in Zenica in an ambulance car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it was during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you be more specific and if you cannot give us the exact date, if you could just tell us in what month it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was in late January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you describe the situation, the circumstances under which that patient was transferred to the medical centre in Zenica and if you can tell us what happened on that particular occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had a number of injured, wounded patients, people who were injured during the conflict and they were transported in one of our ambulance cars to the hospital in Zenica. On the way back, the vehicle was requisitioned and the driver was harassed. And after that we no longer sent patients to that medical institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you say that the vehicle was requisitioned and the driver was harassed, do you know who was it that requisitioned the vehicle and harassed the driver?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were the fighters of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This ambulance that you used to transport patients from Busovaca to Zenica, did they have any signs on it? Did it have any signs on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the vehicle had a Red Cross sign and it was written, Busovaca Health Centre on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After this vehicle was requisitioned, how many vehicles did you still have at the health centre in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many, I believe there was only one vehicle that was in good condition, but I am not sure, one, or maybe two. But very often the vehicles wouldn't be in good condition because they were quite old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As far as you can remember, did you have enough spare parts and fuel for these vehicles during the first half of 1993? So I am still referring to the period of when the armed conflict broke out on the territory of the Municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In January we were still receiving fuel from reserves that could be found at the municipality. After that, it was getting difficult, so when we had a number of injured people, we would usually have to wait for two or three of them so that we can transport them to hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, do you remember the beginning of the conflict on the territory of the Busovaca municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The conflict started on Sunday, on the 5th. And it lasted, I am not quite sure, but I believe it was for about ten days. This was the first conflict. And a week later, at the beginning of February, another conflict broke out. And, in total, I think that one can say that the conflict lasted for about one month with several lapses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You've mentioned the date, the 5th of January, 1993, and you indicated that it was the beginning of the conflict on the territory of the Busovaca municipality, do you have any particular event in mind that made you pick that specific date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that day, I was at home and at around 6.00 a.m., I woke up, I heard a loud explosion, detonation, coming from the direction of Kacuni. And later on I heard that Ivica Petrovic had been brought to the medical centre. And another body, a body of an unknown person. Two bodies, therefore, have been brought from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know exactly what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as the area of Kacuni is concerned, I think that these people were ambushed by the BiH soldiers. Petrovic was a policeman. They were attacked and later they were killed. Petrovic was wounded and then he was stabbed to death with a knife. And this other person, I think was killed as a result of explosion, but I don't remember exact details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us more about that, do you know where exactly they were attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the exact location, but I believe it was in the area of Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it was at their homes or on the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were ambushed and attacked on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you personally see these two bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only saw Petrovic's corpse, I didn't see the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, at that time, was there a morgue in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't have any on that day, but because the conflict had broken out, we had to arrange, we had to find something, so we did have a makeshift morgue, which was first located near the post office and then later on it was moved to the forestry office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the morgue was not part of the medical centre in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, you were working as a physician at the medical centre in Busovaca, could you tell us in general terms how many patients were treated at the Busovaca medical centre before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean daily?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And after the conflict broke out, could you tell us how many patients were treated at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at that time, we had a large number of patients. We sometimes had as many as 200 patients a day, mostly civilians, but also wounded soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You've mentioned wounded soldiers, these were the soldiers of which army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were the soldiers of the Croatian Defence Council, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The HVO you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever notice amongst the wounded soldiers any one with insignia of the HV?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I never saw a soldier of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As a patient, but did you ever see Croatian soldiers in the area, in Busovaca in the Town of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, as far as I know there were no soldiers of the Croatian army on the territory of Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you if you saw any, if you ever saw any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I never saw any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, during the second half of the month of January, 1993, you mentioned that you had duty service at your institution, could you describe how it functioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean after the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, after the beginning of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was difficult to organise it because of the number of physicians that were available. During the first ten days of the conflict, Dr. Bernardica Mioc was there on duty, I believe, but after that she left for Zenica. And then there were only three of us left. Dr. Petrovic was ill at the time, so she mostly worked during the morning and I worked the night shift at the beginning, especially at the emergency ward. And sometimes, especially if the conflict was fierce, I would be there all the time. There was also Dr. Raos who would work every two or three days for 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What about Dr. Srdana Markovic, was she there as well at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I forgot about her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So there were four of you at the time, four physicians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct, during the first months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, how many physicians and nurses would work in one shift?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One shift usually included one physician on duty and three nurses on average.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You've indicated a large number of patients that were treated at your health centre, given the situation, did you treat your patients properly in the administrative sense, would you always check their medical insurance card or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, at that time, there was no administration at all. We simply worked with everyone who would come to the institution without any particular checks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Am I correct in thinking that at the time you offered medical help without previously checking whether that the patient had medical insurance or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, do you remember the structure, the national composition, the ethnic composition of the people who used your services?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're referring to the month of January?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The month of January, February, the first half of the year in 1993, was that composition of patients different as opposed to the situation prior to the war? Were there any changes that took place in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because prior to the conflict, Bosniaks, Muslims, that is, had mainly left the Town of Busovaca. Not the territory of the Busovaca municipality in general, but the town itself. There were 5 or 10 per cent Muslims left in the area. The rest were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, did you make any difference as to the standards that were applied while providing medical services? Did you differentiate between patients on the basis of their nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that because I know that there is only one way, one proper way to treat people. As for differentiating, I am not quite clear as to what you wanted to ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were there any differences in treatment of people on the basis of their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, such a situation is simply unthinkable to me, and I couldn't differentiate, discriminate amongst the people on the basis of their nationality or religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, could you please tell us, if you remember, what was the ethnic structure of the staff at the Busovaca health centre towards the end of 1992 and in early 1993, that is about the time when you got the job there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, about half of them were Bosnias, Muslims, a little less than 50 percent. Also a little less than 50 percent were Croats, and there were a few Serbs, a few of them, perhaps five to ten percent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you mentioned that on the eve of the conflict Muslims began to leave the territory of Busovaca. Could you also feel it at the health centre, that is, did they also leave or did they continue with the health centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the eve of the outbreak of the conflict, a day or two perhaps, Bosniaks, Muslims left, that is, did not turn up for work at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How did you -- what did you think of this situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the situation was rather vague -- it was rather muted a few days before the conflict, because the Bosniaks, Muslims were leaving in large numbers. The territory, one could see it with the naked eye, they were saying they were going to attend a fair or something. There were different explanations. But it was quite evident that something was about to happen or something was afoot somewhere. But most of us had no idea what.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When the conflict broke out, did you relate that particular phenomenon with the outbreak of armed conflicts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean after the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I mean after. Did you somehow associate this departure of Muslims from the area with the outbreak of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, clearly. Mostly able-bodied men remained in the territory of the municipality, whereas women and children were all gone from the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, will you tell us if you are familiar with the Kaonik facility in the vicinity of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am. It is a former ammunition depot of the Territorial Defence, the depot of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Since you mentioned the former JNA, could you tell us if in sometime in April '92 the JNA bombed Busovaca. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I do remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what happened at that time with regard to the health centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The health centre was then hit by missiles, so part of the ground floor was destroyed. Also part of the gynaecological wing, that is the gynaecological surgery, was destroyed, and water piping in the ground floor. And we were left without electricity and water supply. Other buildings, other things were also shelled, but this concerned the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to Kaonik, that is the former JNA facility. Do you remember if patients, that is people seeking health services, came to the health centre from that particular facility after the outbreak of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean JNA members?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, I am not talking about JNA members. I am talking about the end of January '93.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did. They began to come towards the end of January and until about, I don't know, sometime early February until they were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, in principle, what complaints did those patients who came from Kaonik have? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were mostly some chronic disorders, usually chronic hypertension patients, stomach or duodenal ulcer. You know, these are stress situations which exacerbate such borderline diseases. There was some infections and some things, but nothing really to talk about, at least from the medical point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who brought those patients to the health centre in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were escorted by guards, and very often there was also Mr. Aleksovski accompanying them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You have mentioned Mr. Aleksovski. So I must ask you, have you met him personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you recognise him if you saw him today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you, perhaps, see Mr. Aleksovski in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the gentleman behind you, the gentleman behind you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For the record, the witness identified the accused as the man sitting behind the Defence bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, when did you meet Mr. Aleksovski for the first time? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember the date, but it could have been the end of January or early February, sometime around that. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the beginning of the conflict in the Municipality of Busovaca, which is the 21st of January. So as against that date, the beginning of the conflict, could you say whether you met Aleksovski -- when did you meet Mr. Aleksovski? Was it before that particular date or was it after it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was after it, after the 25th. So it must have been on one of the ten days after that. I did not know him before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, did Mr. Aleksovski visit to the health centre often or not so often; I mean, when accompanying persons from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in point of fact, he was a relatively frequent visitor. He often accompanied prisoners and sometimes came even without them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you have any personal contact with him, apart from some informal chats? Were there some contacts regarding medical services and the like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, there were contacts. At times he would ask -- well, perhaps not from me, but he asked the health centre personnel to carry out the examination -- well, not during those 10 or 15 days, but later on during the former half of '93, he invited us to inspect the Kaonik facility, what it looked like, whether something could be improved, of course, in view of the conditions that prevailed at the time and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what Mr. Aleksovski wore at the time, what kind of clothes he had in those contacts with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rather informally. At times it was uniform, sometimes he was in civilian clothes, sometimes a combination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a uniform. Did he have any insignia of an army or rank on that uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think he had any kind of markings. I don't think so. I don't remember exactly, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that it was quite casual, that sometimes he was in uniform, sometimes civilian clothes, sometimes a combination of the two. Was this matter of dressing a common thing at the time or was it an exception; I mean, compared with the population in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was quite a common phenomenon, even after the outbreak of the conflict. People often wore those trousers or the jacket because there were -- they were very good work, they could work in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you say trousers or the jacket, you mean the military ones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, you said that those patients who were escorted by guards and brought from Kaonik mostly complained of some chronic disorders. Do you remember how were they brought by the guards? Did you see them being brought in a vehicle and then enter the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did see them. They would be brought in a white van at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were they tied?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were they handcuffed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were not restrained in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you describe the treatment they were accorded at the health centre. As of the moment they would go through the door of the health centre and entered the waiting room, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as regards them, regardless of the large number of patients that we had, we would discontinue the examination of other patients and would take them first. Usually a guard or Mr. Aleksovski would come in and agree with us about it, and then they would enter one by one and we would examine them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did the guard or Mr. Aleksovski, if he happened to escort those patients, stay in the surgery during such examinations or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not always. If we asked for it, but not always. I can't remember, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that when patients were brought from Kaonik that the guard or Mr. Aleksovski, if he accompanied them, would enter the surgery to see about the examination. And the patients at that time, where were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would be in front of the surgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the waiting room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Together with other patients waiting for whatever health service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were they isolated in any way, put in a special room, or were they in the normal, regular waiting room where all the other patients awaited to see the doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no. There is no special room there. It is a passage with some benches and all the patients are there. I mean, we simply did not have any special room and there was no need for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So in that situation when Kaonik patients waited to be admitted into the surgery for whatever health service, medical service, were they under any supervision, or did they just sit there and wait like any other patient?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I do not know. If a guard entered, then they would, presumably, stay there alone with other patients. I don't know. I never checked that. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. Dr. Stipac, you mentioned that patients usually came with some chronic complaints. I am referring to people who came from Kaonik. Do you remember -- can you recall if, apart from those chronic complaints, were there any other complaints or disorders, I mean some bodily injuries, fractures, wounds, things like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bodily injuries. Well, yes, there were such cases. Mostly haematoma, scratches and things like that. Fractures, I don't recall. I don't remember, really, because whenever they would suspect something, we could take an x-ray. So I would presumably remember if there was something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned bruises and scratches, things like that. I am well aware six years have elapsed since, but do you remember, what was the ratio, what was the percentage of such injuries of such health problems as against the overall in number? That is, whether the ratio were very high, were there very many such cases or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not say so. I do not really think it was a widespread phenomenon. Perhaps of five patients, one would perhaps have injuries of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, did you in such situations, that is, of course, if you were the one who was extending them medical help, did you ever ask those patients about such injuries, I don't mean chronic diseases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never discussed it with patients. My duty was to extend aid to them, medical aid to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, do you, perhaps, remember if there was a situation that a patient complained to you personally when he was left alone with you in the surgery, when Mr. Aleksovski or the guard were not there? Did any one of them complain of something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean how they were treated?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, how they were treated or perhaps the cause of these injuries.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't really remember. Maybe they did, but I simply don't remember, because a lot of time has passed by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, you said that in Busovaca there was an improvised morgue which had to be moved twice. Did you ever go there to examine the -- to examine the bodies? I don't mean autopsies, I mean simply to see the bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this was a very painful sight. Dr. Petrovic, Dr. Ruzica, they were not simply up to it. Their health would not permit them. So it was always Dr. Raos and I who went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: During those examinations, do you, perhaps, remember an occurrence when you examined two bodies of two citizens of Muslim origin who had been brought to that morgue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were two bodies brought to the morgue of two citizens of Muslim origin. I don't remember that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let me rephrase it. Did anyone ask you to look at those two bodies and make a record of the injuries, make a practical of the injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that two Bosniak Muslims were killed on a job and a lot of dust was raised about this, so that Mr. Aleksovski requested us to make the record of the causes of death. And I do not remember what their injuries were and who did it, but it was a rather singular event. So I remember it. I don't remember that anything like that happened after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that was Mr. Aleksovski who requested you to conduct the examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. There had been -- they had been detained and they were under his supervision, and therefore they fell under his jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened subsequently, or you have no knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you, perhaps, remember the injuries on those two dead bodies? What did they die of, or is it that you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't, to be quite frank. I simply don't remember. I remember the -- that particular event, but the injuries, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, you mentioned that you had been to see the Kaonik facility in person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you describe the circumstances under which you visited it, and whose initiative was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we went there only when invited by Mr. Aleksovski, whether to examine a patient, to inspect the facility, various reasons. Could be different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Since you mentioned inspection of the facility, what do you mean by that? Was the purpose of such inspections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we had more of an advisory, consultative role, how to improve the sanitary conditions of the facility and such like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, when you were on the duty service, on the emergency service at the time, did you ever come across patients suffering from some infectious disease? I mean some infection or perhaps some contagious disease.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean from the facility? Perhaps there were a case here and there, but nothing that would look like an outbreak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you say "a case here and there," sporadic cases, what disease do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean mostly those caused by parasites, that is scabies, but they often arrived at the facility with such a particular disease, so it was rather simple to treat, and we then undertook measures to suppress them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And did these -- did the state of their health, was it a major variance with the state of health of the population at large?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think there were much more cases of scabies among the HVO forces, because of course the conditions in the trenches were abominable, so that on that side we could even be talking about an epidemic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mean the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean the HVO combatants.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, what facilities did you visit in Kaonik, and how many times did you go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How many times? I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, was it once or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several times, two or three, perhaps, I don't know, five. What was your first question? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What facilities did you visit there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I visited the prison, that is where the cells were. As a matter of fact, nothing else, only that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what was your business there? Why did you go there? Was it simply to extend some medical help or was it something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By and large it was for medical reasons, I remember, and an injured patient who had been hospitalised in Nova Bila, and when his -- when his health stabilised he was transferred to Kaonik, but Penicillin treatment was continued. And since there may be problems with Penicillin, then the nurse there would go there to administrate to him to avoid anything -- I mean, the patient had been wounded and transportation wouldn't have good for him. So that we went instead to see him from the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was your impression as a physician about the conditions in that facility in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't a facility built for the purpose. And my impression was that they had done quite a lot to make it a viable place, a place where one could really -- a little more or less decently. But I really don't know. I don't know what I could compare it with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have an opportunity to see the toilets in Kaonik, bathrooms, laboratories?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did. I don't really remember them all that well, but it worked, more or less. It was cleaned. I don't really know what I could say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What did you think about those patients from Kaonik that you treated as regards the diet, the state of health in general, their physical appearance, the hygiene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they did not starve. They were not undernourished. It was warm, as far as I can remember, because I believe there were one or two big stoves which then heated the whole facility. There were not any serious diseases, serious disorders among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever talk to some of those people in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, what were the circumstances in general? We are still in the former half of '93. What was the situation, what were the circumstances in the Municipality of Busovaca? By this, I mean water supply, power supply, food supply, clothes, footwear, medicines and the rest. Could you, perhaps, describe the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were not the same throughout the former half of '93. At the outset we had some medicine, that is some stocks, left behind, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did you want to say --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: With this question, Your Honours, it is going outside the ambit of the indictment, because the question relates to the former half of -- the second half of 1993, as far as I understand it. If that is the case, my objection is that the question is outside the terms, outside the time frame of the indictment, which is January to May 1993, Your Honours. Yes, he refers to the second half of 1993, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, do you have anything you would like to add on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your lordships, I think it was simply a mistake. I am not asking anything about the second half of '93. My questions all relate to the former half of '93, and even if it was not the mistake in translation, then perhaps I might have made a slip of the tongue. At any rate, my questions all relate to the former half of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I withdraw my objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may resume your questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your lordship.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, let me remind you. The question was what were the -- what was the situation in the Municipality of Busovaca, in which you also lived in the former half of '93, regarding electricity, water, food supply, clothes, footwear, medicines, et cetera? Could you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In point of fact, in the former half of '93 there were no supplies. We lived off stocks for the food, electricity. Well, sometimes there were some cuts, some not. Water supply, again depended on the part of the town. Some did not have water, some did. Those parts which were controlled by the Army of the BiH, their water supply was cut off. Other parts of the town did have running water. Well, no luxury, of course. There was rationing since nothing was coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How did you get the medicines? Only the stocks or were there some donations or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't really know much about that, because it was the director who took care of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the light of the situation as regards the supply, was the health centre in the same situation as all the other institutions and the citizenry in the Municipality of Busovaca, or did you have some additional sources of supply?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the health centre, supply of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Everything, all the basic necessities and medicines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We lived under the same conditions as everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, do you know, when it comes to the preparation of food, where was the food prepared for the prisoners in Kaonik? Where was it prepared and transported to them? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think it was prepared at the Draga and then it was transported, delivered to Kaonik two or three times a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the same food was taken somewhere else from that barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the food was taken to the soldiers who were at the frontline and also to the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the medical centres, soldiers at the frontline, at the prison facility, that they all had the same food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, you mentioned that you went to school, secondary school in Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, were you ever in a position to provide medical help to some of your professors from the grammar school in Vitez, people who would be brought there as patients?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I remember they were Professor Enes Surkovic and Kadir Dzidic. They used to be my professors at the grammar school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who brought them to the medical centre and what were the circumstances of this event? Could you describe it for us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were detained at the Kaonik facility and I don't know why, but anyway, they were brought to the medical centre under the escort of some guards. I wanted to talk to them, because I wanted to ask them if they needed anything because I was in very good terms with my secondary school professors, secondary school teachers. But the situation was a bit awkward.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what kind of complaints they had, why was it that they came to the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember any specific reasons. I believe that they were under stress. They suffered from insomnia. I don't think that they suffered from any specific medical disease. It's difficult to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was a long time ago, I understand. You've indicated that you would sometimes provide advice when requested to do so by Mr. Aleksovski regarding the situation at the Kaonik facility, what kind of advice was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would simply advise him as to the measures, medical measures that were to be taken at the facility, such as fumigation, rat extermination. That the facility should be fumigated against rats and the toilet facilities should be disinfested and so on, whatever was our field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the medical centre ever conducted any kind of intervention in that sense? Did they conduct fumigation or rat extermination at the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they conducted such actions, I don't know on how many occasions. It was the head nurse that was in charge of that, but I don't know who exactly took part in fumigation and rat extermination that were conducted at the Kaonik facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, with the assistance of the usher, I would like to show you some documents, medical documents. And I would kindly ask you to have a look at them. This is Exhibit No. 18 and I would kindly ask the usher to present them in order and to use the ELMO. And Dr. Stipac, I would ask you, because you know the handwriting of your doctors and because of your profession, I would like you to interpret these documents for us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In order?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would kindly ask the usher to place them one by one on the ELMO so that we can see the document on the monitor. Dr. Stipac, do you have the document on your monitor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it just disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It will come back again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see it now. The name is Ilijas Krivosija. Herniated disk, therapy recommended, to be spared from work and to lie on flat surface. Do you need any other interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, please. What is a herniated disk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a degenerative disorder of the spine and the therapy that is most often recommended is antirheumatic and the patient should always lie on flat surface, although the therapy medication is not indicated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, is this a chronic disease or an acute disease?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a chronic disease with acute exacerbations. We can speak of a chronic disease here. It lasts for a long time. It's a degenerative process. And from time to time the patient has pains, which can be calmed down, but which are likely to reappear if the patient lifts say, for example, something heavy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you by any chance know this patient?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know Ilijas Krivosija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know when this document was issued? Is there anything that you could base your conclusion on in the document? Have a look at the signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was issued by Dr. Bernardica Mioc. I believe that the document was issued at the beginning, during the first days of the conflict, between the 25th of January and the end of that month.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can we see the next document, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The name is Avdo Husbasic, status (inaudible)-- at the section of the stomach. The method used was (inaudible) anaemia, high pressure, high blood pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What about the second part, is it hernia again, second part of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's quite difficult to read it. A, B. Yes, I think it's hernia, abdominals, in the area of the abdomen. Again, it's a chronic disease. The patient is supposed to rest, be on diet. The medication prescribed was Ramatal, two times one tablet. Amocil. And home treatment was also requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know this patient personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The name rings a bell, but I couldn't remember who that person was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Judging from the name of the doctor who issued the document, could you tell us which period this document refers to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's no date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the original, the seal of the doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the signature of Dr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, can we have the next document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Name inaudible), lumbar (term in B/S/C). It's also some kind of protrusion of the lumbar disk, lumbar disk, and chronic ulcer of the duodenum. Therapy is indicated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know this patient?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know him personally, but I know that he was a high school teacher. I know him by sight. He's an acquaintance. I can't say that I know him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Which high school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The high school in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether this person was brought as a patient from the Kaonik facility or you have no knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, can we have the next document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ejub Buljina. There's a code for diagnosis, according to the old categorisation. I think it refers to weakness of heart muscle, four to five. Home treatment is recommended. It's probably a chronic disease with some kind of acute exacerbation with all the symptoms of the disease and it is only logical that the doctor requested home treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know this patient personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Next document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is illegible, Svad Halilovic. It's a contused -- it's an injury of the chest, but without fracture, so I believe that an x-ray must have been done. Therapy recommended, home treatment again. I know this patient. People called him "Suvi" in Busovaca. Suvi because he was tall and skinny and he still is that way. I know him and I know that he was detained at the time and that he was brought to the health centre by guards. I remember him because I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the next document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hasan Pezic. We have a code again. I think that the patient had problems with circulation with veins, varicose veins, compresses were indicated as therapy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What kind of disease is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a disease of the veins, varicose veins.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it a chronic disease?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's a chronic disease. It develops over a number of years, decades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know this patient personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know him. This is a very common surname in Busovaca and I know him personally. Nasic Silajdic, swelling in the area of the left ear, earache. It was an infection of the middle ear, therapy is indicated here. The patient had to avoid contact with water. I can't read this. Draught, yes, draught.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know this patient. I know some of them by name, but I don't know them personally. Dervic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the document on the ELMO, maybe that would be easier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Senad Dervic, 5, 3, 2, duodenal ulcer. Again, we have a case of duodenal ulcer. The therapy is indicated. The patient had to rest. Again, it's a chronic disease.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know this patient?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the name tells me something, but I know him by name, but not personally. He's an elderly man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The document was issued by Dr. Bernardica Mioc on the 26th of January, 1993, this is the period when she was on duty, when she was working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see the next document, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't see the name. Yes, Lusija, Ethem Lusija. This is an examination of the ear. Here we have a case of high pressure. I know this particular patient. I know him as a patient and I know him from before. He's a very well-known person in our town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What kind of disorders are these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's just high blood pressure. Extrasystole disorder of the heart. An ECG was probably done because, otherwise, the doctor couldn't have reached this diagnosis. The therapy here is administered. I think that after the patient took medication, the doctor must have taken his blood pressure again because here we have it, it's indicated two times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know if this particular person was brought from Kaonik as a patient?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so. I am not quite certain, but I think that he was one of the detainees. But I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can we see the next document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hasan Pezic. I can't read this. There are some portions that were crossed out. Amoxil was administered. Again, the same disease, the same disorder as before. But I think we have an acute inflammation of varicose veins here, that's why the antibiotics were administered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, this document that is in front of us, is different from other documents because it is a form. What kind of form is it, can you explain this to the Court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a form that was used for prescriptions until the conflict. This is the kind of form that we would use to prescribe medication before the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Why do you say that, why do you say that they were used until the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were used -- we used them as long as we had them. And then after the conflict broke out, we had to use something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, we can see on this form that not everything has been filled out. How do you explain that? I am referring to the number of the insurance policy and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was issued on the 27th of January. And during that time, we did not have proper administration. People would simply get a prescription and get their medication directly at the health centre. So this particular information was not important during the war. It was important before the war because it all went through the medical insurance company and so on. But this particular data were no longer important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So whenever patients needed some medication they would get it at the pharmacy which was part of the health centre, which was located at the health centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can we see the last document from this group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Salih Hodzic, the code is 425, Isoptin was prescribed. A heart condition again because of the medication, Isoptin, Salih Hodzic. This person used to work at the institution for medical insurance. I don't know him personally. I know him only by sight. Yes, home treatment, absolutely home treatment. Yes, it's a heart condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether this person was brought from Kaonik or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may add, he probably was brought from Kaonik, because otherwise home treatment would not be specifically indicated. He was probably detained and doctor requested for home treatment for this particular patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have finished with these documents. Dr. Stipac, you've now had an opportunity to see a number of documents from the medical centre and very often home treatment was indicated as therapy, home treatment, rest, the patients had to be spared from work and so on. How do you interpret that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had to be spared from work and from any kind of physical activity. And if the home treatment was requested, it was because any home treatment would have been better than the home treatment than they received at the prison facility. It's a common thing to request, any physician should request that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Dr. Stipac, whether this was acted upon accordingly or you have no knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have any specific knowledge of that, but I think that most of the time it was acted upon accordingly. We administered certain therapy and we would check that on a number of occasions, and indeed, that was respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, at the beginning of your testimony you indicated that you've spent your whole life in Busovaca, that is 35 years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A little more, 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay, 36. I will now show you a photograph and I would kindly ask you to tell me what it is. Can I have the assistance of the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Document D-19.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, what kind of photograph is that and where is this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not quite sure. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can remove this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Mikulicic, perhaps there's some problem with the way in which this photograph was placed? No?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (No translation.) We wanted to see whether the witness can indicate what this area was, but if we cannot, we wouldn't pursue that any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: If you, yourself, are not going to insist upon that, very well. But, perhaps, if we were to turn the photograph, then he'd agree, perhaps. Then, perhaps, the witness will be able to make some comments. Would you like to try that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your suggestion, Your Honour. Maybe this is a good idea, maybe we can turn the photograph upside down and maybe the witness can have a look at it once again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a factory as far as I can see. I am not very good at reading maps and this is probably an aerial photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No luck. Thank you. Thank you, anyway. It can be removed from the ELMO and I would like to tender this into evidence as D-19, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Mikulicic, do you have many more questions left or should we take a recess now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Only one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In my last question for you, Dr. Stipac, it concerns medical control. You have indicated you told us that you followed the situation with your recommendations as to regarding patients at the Kaonik facility and that you checked on several occasions whether the medications were given. Do you remember whether patients were ever brought to the medical centre for check ups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were regularly brought for check ups whenever it was indicated, whenever it was requested. They respected all our recommendations and instructions and I think that in that regard our can operation was very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Stipac, this concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Very well, we shall take a twenty minute recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, you have the floor to continue, I believe. Mr. Meddegoda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: May I proceed? Witness, before the recess and in the course of your testimony you said that you had the opportunity to provide medical help to two of your professors in the grammar school in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And one of them was professor Enes Surkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And who was the other professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kadir Dzidic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now, where was this medical help provided by you to professor Dzidic and professor Surkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Health centre in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And when -- do you remember when they were brought to the health centre in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you remember whether they were brought together or were they brought on two separate occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Together. They were brought together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And you also said that they were brought under the escort of guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: As far as you are aware, doctor, do you know whether professor Surkovic and professor Dzidic have been involved in any military activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that. From Vitez, I don't know what was happening to them during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: As far as you are aware, were professor Surkovic and professor Dzidic involved in any criminal activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. As a matter of fact, I have not seen them for quite a long time before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And as professors who had taught you, you would have had the highest respect for them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you visited the Kaonik camp several times.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I visited the prison on a couple of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: On those occasions -- sorry, I withdraw that question, Your Honour. On those occasions, when you visited the camp, you said that you visited the building with the cells.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true. That is the only building in the prison that I visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You did not visit a hangar building that was in the camp component?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nowhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, you said you commenced work in the Busovaca Health Centre in January 1993. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And at that time you began an internship in the Busovaca Health Centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The internship.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what was the duration of your internship?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So this means that throughout the year of 1993 you worked in the Busovaca Health Centre as an intern, in the course of an internship?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And as far as I recollect, you also said that you worked in the night-shift, or you had night duty in the Busovaca Health Centre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Throughout this period was it the night-shift that you worked on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not always. It depended on the health of other doctors, on the timetable, on the schedule, or when who could work or not. You know, the times were not normal. I worked when it was necessary to and like everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So did you, apart from the night-shift, the night duty, did you also work during the day in the Busovaca Health Centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, often -- I would often be there for 24 hours, sometimes even longer, if there had been any conflict, if there was any fighting, so there were wounded or so on and so forth. We had no working hours. We were there whenever it was necessary. And I live very near to the health centre, perhaps some 50 metres away from it, so they were to call me whenever it was needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know where Dr. Bernardica Mioc is presently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: She is not working in the health centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. She was there -- she was there part-time. She came for a weekend for part-time and then stayed a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When did she come for part-time and stay for a week, during which period was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Saturday and Sunday when the conflict commenced, or perhaps on Sunday she worked for 24 hours. And then she simply could not go back because of the conflict in Zenica, because she normally lived and worked in Zenica, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Does this mean that she did not work -- does this mean that she did not work during the week, but only worked during the weekends?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, she would come there to work part-time because -- I don't really -- I think it was only for weekends, but I can't really remember her timetable. I mean, of course it was subject to her agreement with the director.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And who was the director of the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vesna Bilic, master of sciences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know where Dr. Markovic is at present, witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think she's here in the Netherlands. I'm not sure, but I think she is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And have you -- do you know where Dr. Petrovic presently is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. She's in Busovaca. She's with the health centre. She's a gynaecologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Apart from these doctors, were there others who worked in the Busovaca Health Centre during the period of the conflict from January to May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was Dr. Kordic there, but only for one hour or two in the morning, as she suffered a stroke, a repeated stroke. That is a stroke which she suffered once again during the war, so that she had to stop working altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you remember if there was a Dr. Muhamed Mujezinovic who was working in the Busovaca Health Centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was with the health centre in Vitez, not in Busovaca. I heard about him, but I do not know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Perhaps you are not aware that he worked -- you don't know whether he worked during the period of April to May, 1993, in the Busovaca Health Centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do know he did not work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Doctor, is there any other medical facilities in Busovaca other than the Busovaca Health Centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was an office within the Nova Bila Hospital, but there were only cots there without any doctors. And doctors, surgeons, as a rule, would go from Nova Bila there to see them, treat them. Those were mostly wounded because there was simply not enough room for them all at Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And you said this was in the Nova Bila Hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was in Busovaca, in the kindergarten in Busovaca, but it was attached to Nova Bila Hospital, so that the physicians from Nova Bila Hospital visited it three times a week to control, to check the patients who were hospitalised there. There were several nurses there all the time, but no doctors were attached to that facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And this facility was specifically was for the treatment of HVO soldiers who were wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was for all the wounded. There were civilians too. There was simply not enough room to separate them. That was throughout Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness. You, in the course of your testimony, you referred to two people who were killed and whose bodies were brought to the Busovaca Health Centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. I remember the event, but I don't remember it in any great detail. That is, I don't remember what the injuries were or anything like that. I simply remember the occurrence because it was a singular event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not an autopsy was conducted on either of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The autopsy could not be conducted because conditions for anything like that were lacking. So they could only examine it superficially, that is, describe the superficial injuries and indicate the cause of death. But it was only the superficial examination of the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you remember who conducted that superficial examination of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not exactly. Whether it was me or somebody else, I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: If it was you, you would remember having conducted a superficial examination of these two bodies, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I did so many superficial examinations of injuries, so that whether this was part of that or not, I really don't remember. It must have been one hundred or maybe two hundred such descriptions, so that I really do not know what I did or what I didn't. I really don't. I know that we were asked to do it, but who that was, I really don't know. Perhaps it was me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And do you know whether there was a record of such examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It had to be. But every description of whatever body needed to be typed, put on records, of course, of the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And filed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And that record would, perhaps, be available in the Busovaca Health Centre registers or records?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I guess so. One copy stayed with the health centre and a copy of it was turned over to the police for every body that was on record there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, may the witness be -- I would like to refer the witness to some of the records, Your Honour, that have been produced, marked D18. Could the usher please show to the witness Exhibit D18/F.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, in respect of this patient, the therapy has been recommended and also medication has been recommended. Andol is the medicine that has been recommended to this patient?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And for what illness would Andol be recommended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Andol has many uses. In this case we are dealing with thrombosis of the lower leg vena. It is a good anticoagulant agent. It prevents the blood coagulation so that will prevent the thrombosis developing in those veins. This is standard therapy for such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And the diagnosis in this case has been classified as 454?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the old nomenclature. It was not in use in '93. But I should say that it was the varicose veins of the lower leg. So varicose veins of the crural vein, I guess, in the crural region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now, in respect of such patients, would you recommend antibiotics on occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It only depended whether the veins were inflamed or not. I mean, if there was an inflammation, yes. If not, then antibiotics would serve no purpose

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDOGODA
utterances.text: Thank you. I do not think I require the document --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
