utterances.text: I would not require the document any further, document D18/F, and, therefore, that can be taken off the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, you said that patients would be brought to the Kaonik health facility medical centre either by Mr. Aleksovski or, at times, escorted by guards from the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And you also said that they would be brought in and examined, depending on the urgency of the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean, urgency of the situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: If a patient is brought, is he immediately brought into the examination room or to the surgery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we usually examine them straight away. I mean, those who would be brought in. It was simply more practical for us and for the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who would bring them into the surgery or the examination room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they came -- either escorted by guards or by themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And before they were brought into the room, was it practice for you to talk to the escort or to the guard or to Mr. Aleksovski who would bring them to the Busovaca Health Centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He would merely announce -- he would simply announce that they had so many patients for examination and whether we could see them straight away. And that is what we did. There were no other conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And in the examination theatre or in the examination hall, room, you said you wouldn't talk to the patient about the cause of illness or the cause of the injury or the cause of his complaint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no. No. Not as a rule, because it could only embarrass the patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no more questions in cross-examination from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Meddegoda. Mr. Mikulicic, do you have any more questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your lordship. No, we have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Dr. Stipac, this is the end of your testimony before this International Tribunal. Thank you for coming and testifying, and we wish you a pleasant return to your country. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, do you have another witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour. The Defence would like to call Ms. Blazenka Stapic. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, madam. Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You will now read the solemn declaration, which the Court usher has before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You are now going to respond to the questions put to you by Mr. Mikulicic, who is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Stapic. I am Counsel for the accused, Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski, in this case, and I would like to ask you several questions and kindly ask you to answer them to the best of your recollections. Are you seated comfortably?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If it is easier for you, you can lean on the chair, because I think that the microphone is strong enough?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Stapic, you are related, but I have to ask you your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 8th of September '55 in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you always live in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've always lived in Busovaca. In the Village of Skradno, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you live in the Village of Skradno. This is outside the town of Busovaca itself?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How far is it, approximately, from Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Stapic, what is your educational background?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I completed my elementary education in Busovaca and the secondary medical school in Zenica. I specialised in midwifery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I am a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you a religious person? Who is your religion?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I am a Roman Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when it was, when you completed your medical education in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: It was in 1984.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What did you do after high school? Did you find a job there?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes. I found a job in 1986, a year and a half after I completed my education.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where was it?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I found a job at the medical centre in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What kind of job did you get?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I got a job as midwife at the gynaecological department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you've been working at the Busovaca Health Centre ever since, from '86?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Stapic, in 1993, the first half of 1993, that is before that period, how many patients would you receive for treatment every day, do you remember that, the statistics?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember the exact statistics, but we did have quite a few patients, but I don't know exactly how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The Busovaca Health Centre is a medical institution which was responsible for which area?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: The area of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the Town of Busovaca or the Municipality of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: The Municipality of Busovaca, including the town itself. There was only one such medical centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Stapic, do you remember how many physicians and how many nurses and assistants were employed at the Busovaca Health Centre at the beginning of 1993, that is before the outbreak of the conflict in Busovaca and the surroundings?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Before the conflict I don't remember exactly how many, maybe there were 15 or 16 nurses and assistants, but I am not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What about the physicians?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I don't know, I couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Stapic, do you remember what happened in April, 1992, with the building of the medical centre, did it suffer any damage at that time?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was shelled with a missile and it was damaged. It was not completely destroyed, but the damage was quite extensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said it was hit with a missile, what exactly do you mean by that? Was it air bombing?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it was an air attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So the aircraft dropped bombs on the medical centre in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know who they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: To the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What kind of damage was it?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, one part, one wing of the building was completely destroyed. We didn't have water because the pipes were destroyed. We didn't have electricity for a period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What happened later on, have there been any repairs, what was the situation in 1993 as a result of that? Could you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, the medical centre was repaired, but I don't remember when exactly it was. I don't know whether it was before this conflict or -- no, no, I couldn't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Stapic, do you remember what was the ethnic structure, ethnic composition of the medical staff at the medical centre in Busovaca prior to the outbreak of conflict in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, all nationalities, ethnicities were represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: There were Muslims, Croats and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to specific figures, could you give us any percentage, how many Croats, how many Muslims and so on?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I think that there were maybe 50 per cent, I am not sure. They were evenly distributed, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You've indicated that you lived in the village of Skradno and that the village is situated 8 kilometres from Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How did you go to work?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: On foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Prior to the outbreak of the conflict, do you remember what the situation was?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you describe for us, please, and tell us if you had any duties, were you on duty before the outbreak of the conflict and what kind of impression did these events leave on you?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: We could feel tension several days before the conflict. I was working at the gynaecological department at that time and we had one duty, night duty per month and I was working before the conflict on night duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the exact date?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I believe it was on the 23rd of January. It was a Saturday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you were on duty that day?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How did it go, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, things were rather quiet at the time. I was on duty together with Dr. Mioc and there was also a cleaning lady who was on duty at the health centre at the time and there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You're referring to Saturday 23rd of January?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of the cleaning lady?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: It was Mrs. Senida.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Senida?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I don't remember her surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was her ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: She was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That day or before that day, did you notice anything strange happening in the municipality and the Town of Busovaca itself? I am referring to the behaviour of the Muslim population in the area.

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: During these several days, the situation was tense. On that day when I was on duty, usually we would first drink coffee in the surgery, together with the physician and the cleaning lady and I remember that this colleague of mine, this cleaning lady, she told me that Muslims were leaving Busovaca. Saturday is a market day in Busovaca and its quite busy, so we went outside and indeed we saw columns of people going in the easterly direction. They were simply moving out, but we didn't know what was happening and we stayed. She told me, "my sister is expected to have a baby. Her mother in law, they're all leaving to Kacuni," it's a village nearby. And indeed seven or eight days later, her sister gave birth at the medical centre, but she was alone at home, her family had left several days before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that it was your colleague, the cleaning lady, who told you about that moving out of the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any specific comments? Did she give any explanation as to why that was happening?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No, she did not. She herself said, I don't know what's happening, it seems that everybody has gone crazy. People are moving out. And we didn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You've mentioned the village of Kacuni. You told us that it was a Muslim village in the vicinity of Busovaca, do you know what happened in the village of Kacuni a day later?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, I was not working that day, but I know that two Croat men were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know their names by any chance?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: One of them was Ivo Petrovic. And the other, he was not from our municipality and I don't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what was the occupation of Ivo Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the circumstances under which these killings took place?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: All I know is what I heard from my colleague who was working that day. She told me that they had been killed in the village of Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you don't have any personal knowledge about that event?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that it was Senida, the cleaning lady, who is a Muslim that drew your attention to the situation to what was happening. She said that she didn't know what was going on, but that the Muslims were leaving Busovaca. What was the situation amongst the employees at the medical centre in Busovaca? You told us that there were lots of Muslims who were employed there, what happened with them?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Our colleagues would not come to work these days, and some had taken some time off and some simply wouldn't show up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So that the record is clear, Mrs. Stapic, when you say "these days," which period exactly do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I am referring to the period two or three days prior to the outbreak of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Two or three days before the conflict, these people, the Muslim employees at the health centre would not come to work?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No, except for one or two colleagues who had taken leave, maybe a week before that or ten days before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand, thank you. Mrs. Stapic, you have direct contact with patients, do you have any knowledge as to the situation with medical supplies at the health centre?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: We had some reserves, but it was our head nurse who was in charge of that. I think that we are received most of the supplies through UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What reserves do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I am referring to the medical supplies that we had at the time that we received after the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you're referring to the second half of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Stapic, was the pharmacy that was located at the medical centre operational at the time?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And where would the patients get their medicine?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: At the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Maybe I was not quite clear, was there any pharmacy that was located within the medical centre in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay. So the procedure was followed and correct me if I am wrong, a patient would receive a prescription and then he would be given medicine at the local internal pharmacy of the health centre?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was that the only pharmacy that was operational at the time?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Stapic, after the outbreak of the conflict and after the events in the village of Kacuni, how would you go to there from the Village Skradno?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: On foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was it safe for you to go to work in these conditions, did you have to be particularly cautious, could you describe the situation?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, it was not safe, but we had this type of obligation, we were supposed to, we had to come to work. There's an old road that we from the village of Skradno would take and other colleagues would take the main road. There was shooting at the time, but we would come to work every day, regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Stapic, in the village of Skradno, do you know what was the ethnic composition of the population, was it predominantly Croat village or a Muslim village or a mixed village?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: It was a mixed village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any fighting around the village of Skradno at that time?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was some fighting. There was shooting, but I don't know where it came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Stapic, when was the first time that you heard about the Kaonik facility? Are you aware of such facility?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, I live in the vicinity and I know that it used to be military barracks, but I had never been to that facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you say that it was a form of barracks, what exactly did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, the JNA army was accommodated there before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Stapic, do you remember when it was that the JNA left the barracks?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what happened after that, do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: You mean after the shelling? I mean we were shelled at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But you personally have never been to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Before and after the conflict?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Stapic, when did you first come across patients who were brought to the Busovaca health centre from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: It was in late January and early February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know the person by the name of Zlatko Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When did you first meet him?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, it was at that time when he started bringing in these people, so it was in late January, early February, at the very beginning of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Stapic, could you recognise, would you recognise Mr. Aleksovski if you saw him today?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you see him here in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where he's sitting?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, he's sitting right behind you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For the record, please, if it can be reflected that the witness has stated that the accused is sitting behind the Defence. Mrs. Stapic, what kind of contact did you have with Mr. Aleksovski, if any?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: He would bring in patients for examination and that's how we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how he was dressed at that time when he would come to the health centre? Did he have an uniform? Was he wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Both, both uniform and civilian clothes. Sometimes he would come dressed in civilian clothes and sometimes he would be in uniform. Sometimes he would come dressed in parts of a uniform. But in any case, it was both, both civilian clothes and uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember him wearing any insignia on his uniform, military insignia or rank insignia?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: We didn't pay any attention to it, but I don't think he had any such insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Stapic, did you notice when Mr. Aleksovski or some other guards would bring in patients from Kaonik, did you observe that, how would they bring in patients, by car, on foot?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: They would bring them by car, in a vehicle. Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski would either come alone or with someone else who worked at the prison facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if these people were constrained or tied up, did they have any handcuffs?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mean you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No, I know that they didn't have any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you please describe for us the procedure that was applied when Kaonik patients were brought into the Busovaca medical centre? What was the follow up procedure? Did you have any?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, this was the only medical centre in the area. And all patients were brought to our centre, but we would always make sure that these people were admitted first. We would take them into our -- to the nurse's office so that there wouldn't be any problems in the waiting area later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I think perhaps Mr. Aleksovski has some problem, you might check with him to see if he's in good health.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Defence is thankful for your concern. My client has just informed me that he's feeling very well. It's just that he's getting a little emotional because of the events that are being described here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Stapic, you said -- problems in the waiting room, what did you mean by this, what kind of problems?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I just said it was the only health centre, both the military and the civilians were coming there. The conflict was already on the way and we wanted to do our job. I was afraid that somebody might hurt somebody while on the premises of the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mrs. Stapic, that there were instances when patients, that is, HVO soldiers who were seeking medical help because of wounds or some other injuries and the patients from Kaonik would find themselves together there around the same time?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, because there was one waiting room and they were all in that same waiting room, but perhaps under some special circumstances, we would move Mr. Aleksovski and his patient to our room, to our examination room where we were, so that that person could be examined immediately and returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. Do you remember if there were any incidents between HVO members and other patients in the waiting room of the health centre?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No, no, not on our premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Stapic, do you remember, what did the Kaonik patients complain of?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: They mostly suffered from various disorders which they had even before. That is either blood pressure, or perhaps, sugar content or headaches and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did it ever happen that one of those people complained to you about how they had been treated?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Stapic, have you ever seen any of these patients that we are talking about, that is those persons brought from Kaonik, did you ever see any one of them injured? I mean, fractures, perhaps or some obvious bruises or other injuries somewhere on the body or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I do not remember any fractures, but I remember a man whom Mr. Zlatko brought in, he had bruises on his back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the surname of that man?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could it be a person whose surname was Sivro, does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I was trying to remember for a long time. It could be that person, I think that gentleman's name was Sivro, but I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to him, did you ask him about those injuries?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did somebody explain, Mr. Aleksovski or somebody else, ask him where he received his injuries?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I know that six years have elapsed since and that I one has difficulty remembering even some pleasant occurrences, let alone such unpleasant ones,. But, nevertheless, I must ask you, do you perhaps remember the name of some other person, your personal acquaintance who had been brought as a patient from Kaonik to the health centre?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, Busovaca is a small town and most of us knew each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Any one in particular?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps only a professor, I remember he came during my shift and I know he had some problems. He had ulcer, but even before the war, and that was Mr. Ismet Medjuseljac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where was he a professor?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: At the Busovaca secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And he was brought when you were on the shift, when you were on duty. Did you talk to this Mr. Medjuseljac?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No, I simply knew him. I knew him from before because he would come for prescriptions for medicine for himself and for his children and we knew each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you said that Mr. Aleksovski in person brought him there?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if on that occasion Mr. Aleksovski asked or requested some special treatment of that individual?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Quite a number of them were referred for home treatment, for treatment at home and I think he was also recommended for treatment at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Stapic, have you heard of some interventions, I mean medical interventions that are performed at the Kaonik facility by personnel of the health centre?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases, but I didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of interventions were they?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, if some medicines had to be taken there or perhaps some injections, then one of us went. I know when Mr. Zlatko would call us, invite us to go there or bring a patient if, for instance, intermuscular injections were to be given, then a nurse would go and administrate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But you were not among those?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Stapic, tell us, in your practice, in the former half of '93, at the health centre in Busovaca, did you see patients, HVO soldiers, who came there for treatment?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what kind of interventions were those I am now talking about HVO soldiers? What kind of interventions?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, do you mean from the prison --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, no, I mean others.

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Those were mostly injuries or other wounds, wounds from firearms and other complaints.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Have you heard or seen a soldier with HV insignia being brought to the health centre?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No, we did not have such insignia and we did not have any other army members at the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But outside the health centre, as you're an inhabitant of Busovaca and you move around there, did you see a soldier with HV markings outside the health centre somewhere?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Stapic, by nature of your profession, you closely communicated with the patients brought from Kaonik, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What is your recollection, what was your impression, your impressions you got about their general state of health? I mean, their general appearance, did you observe signs of any disease or any epidemics among them or whatever?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No, nothing special. Well, perhaps there were -- no, as a matter of fact, they were unshaved, which is normal if one spends two or three days and without shaving. But as for some contagious infectious diseases, there were none.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were there any signs of skin diseases?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember, not on my shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you see they were perhaps undernourished?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No, we partook of the same food, both the health centre and the prison had the same food. I mean, it came from the same kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, I do. All people under labour obligations, received food from those barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of barracks was it?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: It was the barracks by the name of Draga.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where is this Draga barracks?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well it is above it, perhaps a kilometre and a half or two kilometres above Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In what direction?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Towards Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Stapic, would you tell us, you've already described how medical help was extended, how the Kaonik patients were treated, but could you tell me, did you, being on the medical personnel, did you differentiate, did you make a distinction between these and some other patients as to the regards the help they received?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No, no, there was absolutely no distinction made because we never paid any attention to ethnic origin or asked about someone's name. We would first help that individual and after that we would note their particulars down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you or do you know if any one on the health centre personnel who refused to extend medical help to a patient?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let's go back for a moment to that particular segment of time when patients were brought from Kaonik to the health centre. Do you remember if they were brought one by one or in groups?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, sometimes, at times one by one, sometimes in groups. At times two or three would come together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were they then escorted by several guards, that is, somebody else in addition to Mr. Aleksovski, or only one guard, that is only Mr. Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: At times Mr. Aleksovski only, and at times another guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And did Mr. Aleksovski and the guard enter the examination room, the surgery, or did the patients come in by themselves?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Only the patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does it mean that you were alone with patients?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you recall a case when patients complained to you about something or tried to draw your attention to something that was not something -- something that was not all right, something that was not proper?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Not to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Stapic, you said you lived in the village of Skradno. I think the transcript misstated the distance from Busovaca. Could you repeat, please, what is the distance between Skradno and Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Two kilometres. Thank you. We have no more questions for this witness, Your Lordships.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Madam Stapic, you are now going to respond to Mr. Niemann. We thought about taking a break at 12.10. Perhaps we might take the break now, and then you may cross-examine the witness thereafter. Very well, we will take a 20-minute recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Madam Stapic, now you will respond to questions that will be put to you by Mr. Niemann representing the Prosecutor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, please

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mrs. Stapic, I just wanted to ask you some questions about the town you come from, or the village, Skradno. Was that a predominantly Croatian village or a predominantly Muslim village? What was the majority?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Skradno was 50 percent Muslim and 50 percent Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So about the same.

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned, you spoke of Muslims leaving in particular Busovaca, but did you see Muslim people also leaving Skradno?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Some were leaving Skradno, yes, but a number of Muslims remained in our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And of those that left, did you know any of them personally? Were they friends or associates in any way?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes. My acquaintances and my friends, but I don't remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know -- did you discuss with them the reason why they were leaving? Was that ever mentioned at that time?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No, because we didn't know anything at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, those people that left your village, did they ever come back, or they stayed away all the time?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: They are coming back now. This started a month ago, two months ago. They started coming back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why are they coming back now? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And those that are coming back, are they moving into their houses or are they moving into new ones or different ones?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: They are coming back to their houses, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the course of the war in 1993, were you aware of or did you know of the existence of trenches being placed around Skradno?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know that conflicts were taking place in the immediate vicinity of Skradno?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No. There were no conflicts before the 25th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I am talking about after January 25th.

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I haven't understood you. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question. After the 25th of January, were you aware that there was military conflict going on in trenches around and near the vicinity of Skradno?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: There was no fighting in the area where I lived. There was shooting, but I didn't know where it came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. Did you see any of the Muslim people that had left Skradno return to that village or return to the vicinity of that village during the course of the war in the early part of 1993?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: They started coming back only recently, this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you stay in Skradno during the conflict or did you move into Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have a house in the village of Skradno, and I didn't move out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And it was quite safe, was it, for you to travel from Busovaca down to Skradno and back and forth each day?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No, it was not safe. But we went anyway. One of our colleagues was even wounded on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know a person that came to the clinic by the name of Hamdo Dautovic?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How many nurses were in the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Maybe about 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you work night-shifts or day-shifts, or was it a mixture?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: We worked -- we would work for 24 hours and then we would be free, off duty, for 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember an occasion when a prisoner came from the Kaonik Prison to the medical centre and he was so badly injured that he had trouble walking, couldn't walk from the car? Do you remember any incident like that?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No. Not while I was on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just going back to the time when you say that you saw columns of people, Muslim people, leaving Busovaca. Can you remember what day that was or date that was?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: It was a Saturday and I think that it was the 23rd of January or a day before that. It was a Saturday. I believe it was on the 23rd of January, 1993, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when these people were in the column and leaving Busovaca, did you see any policemen about or any soldiers with them, or marching with them, beside them, or escorting them?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Saturday is market day in Busovaca and the town gets rather crowded. And this is something that I did not observe -- that I didn't observe until my colleague told me when we were in the laundry, when she told me that Muslims were leaving to -- leaving for the neighbouring Muslim villages. And at that point we got out, our physician and this colleague of mine, we got out of the building and indeed we saw people leaving, women and children, people taking cattle away. There was no escort whatsoever, police or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Not that you could see. Did you see where the column ultimately went to, or did you just see it as it went past?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: On the road -- the road they took leads only to the village of Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when these people were in the column leaving the town, were there men with them or was it just women and children?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: There were men as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And why were they leaving Busovaca? Why were these Muslim people in the column leaving Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you ever ask anyone why they were leaving?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, later on, after everything happened, after the outbreak of the conflict, then it all became clear to us. But on that Saturday we didn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the men that were in Busovaca, the Muslim men? Do you know what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Some were leaving and some stayed in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you know now, of course, that some went to Kaonik Prison?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the people that went to Kaonik Prison, the men that you saw during the period of the conflict, did you know them, any of them?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: On that day when the conflict broke out, I was at home, so I didn't know what was happening in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But did you know any of the -- know personally any of the men, the Muslim men that were in Kaonik Prison?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I knew them, but I don't know who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I know you didn't go there, but of the people that you knew to be in Kaonik Prison, that's what I am asking about. These people were people of good reputation and good citizens of the area, were they, prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, I used to know my neighbours and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did any of your neighbours go to Kaonik Prison?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I can't remember their names right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not asking you to remember their names. I know it's hard to do that. But the neighbours that went to Kaonik Prison that you can't remember their names, they were, apart from being Muslim, they were good citizens of the area, I take it?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: They were. We didn't have any problems prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And so whenever they came to the clinic, the prisoners came to the clinic for medical treatment, there was no need for them to be tied up or restrained, because they weren't criminals, were they?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No, they were not tied up at the medical centre. They were not brought into the medical centre in handcuffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Have you ever had prisoners, I am talking about prisoners who had been convicted of serious crimes, brought into your medical centre during any time, any part of your experience, other than this period when the Muslim prisoners were being brought there?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So this is your only experience with prisoners?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that a lot of the prisoners had chronic type ailments which they had had for some time, but I take it that some of them were injured as well that you saw, some of the Muslim prisoners that were brought in from Kaonik had been injured?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember one of them who had bruises on his back. I'm not sure what his name was, but I think that his surname was Sivro.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you would have, from your experience during the war, have gained some experience in determining what are war wounds, people who injure themselves in war, like bullet wounds and those sorts of flesh wounds? I take it, you've got some experience in that?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And it would be easy now, from your experience, to differentiate between people who had war wounds and people who had the sort of illnesses and injuries that came from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: It was the first time that we came across such -- this type of injuries. Of course I know the difference between wounds and other ailments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Did you ever find out -- you mentioned a gentleman by the name of Ismet Medjuseljac, if I've got his name correctly, Medjuseljac. You said he had an ulcer. Do you know what it was that exacerbated or made his ulcer worse such that he needed medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I know that he came to see the doctor, and I know him personally. However, I don't remember what exactly it was the doctor prescribed. I believe it included home treatment. Anyhow, our doctor and we, we did what was our duty. I don't know whether it was all done later on at home and whether it was carried out. I don't know. We couldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know why home treatment was considered so important for these people who had come from Kaonik Prison?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, it's the doctor's decision as to who should receive home treatment. If the doctor says so, prescribes home treatment, then this should be respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I accept that. But my question is really do you know why the doctors considered home treatment important for people who were at the Kaonik Prison?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, so that they could have better conditions. I mean, it would have been better for them to be at home, and so that adequate therapy can be applied and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said that some of them were unshaved, this is the prisoners that had been brought from Kaonik Prison. Were some of them -- were they dirty as well as being unshaved, that you could see?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, some of them had dirty clothes, maybe because they wouldn't change their clothes for two or three days, but this is normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you spoke of the fact that you ate the same food that went to the prison. What was the food? Could you describe the food that you ate at the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: We received food, cooked food in parts. Usually we would have beans, rice, pasta, potatoes. It would have been kind of stew most of the cases, cooked food in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you said that this was provided to all people who had labour obligations. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, did you understand the prisoners in Kaonik to have labour obligations at that time?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I take it, the guards would have had labour obligations? Is that true, the guards would have been people who had labour obligations, guards at Kaonik Prison?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I suppose, because you didn't go to Kaonik, you really couldn't tell me whether or not the guards were the only people to get the food as opposed to the prisoners, or if anything happened to the food, diluted or changed in any way? You couldn't tell me that, could you?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know how the people -- the prisoners at Kaonik were selected for medical treatment? Did you find that out at any stage? If you don't understand my question, say so, and I'll explain.

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: We examined persons who were brought to us. As to how they were selected, I couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mentioned in the evidence Dr. Mioc. Do you know Dr. Mioc at all? Have you ever kept contact after the war, when Dr. Mioc left?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You don't know where Dr. Mioc is now?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about Dr. Markovic? Have you kept contact with Dr. Markovic?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember at any stage during 1993, Dr. Mujezinovic from Vitez coming down and working at the clinic there, Muhamed Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't have a physician. No, he didn't come to our centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe only one question with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please go ahead, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us if you as a nurse working at the medical centre in Busovaca, if you ever found yourself in a situation where patients who were brought in from Kaonik, that they knew on what grounds they were being kept at Kaonik? Were they criminals serving sentence, undergoing some sort of disciplinary measures or were they just civilians who were detained at Kaonik and could you personally distinguish between these categories?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: They were civilians who were accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, but do you know on what grounds? Could you tell that as part of the contact that you had with them at the time, were you aware of that, of the reasons why?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, we have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Madam Stapic, do you know what was the ethnic origin of the patients who came from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: You mean their nationality?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: No, what was the ethnic origin, whether or not whether they were Muslims or Serbs or Croatian?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Were they exclusively Muslim?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Another thing, Madam Stapic, do you have the impression that these patients also knew what your ethnic origin was?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: We knew each other very well, so I think they knew, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Another question, Madam Stapic. You just answered to Mr. Mikulicic that you did not know the reasons for which, inter alia, the person that you knew well, the reasons as I said, the reasons for which these persons were in Kaonik. But do you know or did you know whether they were your neighbours and perhaps you knew their lives very well, did you know whether or not these persons had committed any criminal acts to be placed in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what these people had done. We were doing our job simply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In any case, when you state that they were your neighbours, what distance did they live in relation to your home, approximately?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Maybe 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But, in any case, you say that you do not know why these people were in Kaonik, I am referring inter alia to the persons that you personally knew? Let me ask you this question another way. Did you have any Croat neighbours who were Croatian like yourself?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: And you did not talk with your Croat neighbours about why these persons were in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: On that first day when the conflict broke out, there was shooting coming from the surrounding villages and there was chaos in the town and then, simply, I mean HVO soldiers detained these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Perhaps you might know that the persons that you knew were at Kaonik because the soldiers brought them there?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, the conflict has just begun and they were taken to Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Madam Stapic, you have just completed your testimony here before this International Criminal Tribunal. We'd like to thank you for coming and appearing here before us and we wish you a pleasant return trip to your country. Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Lordships, we should like to call our next witness, Mrs. Ankica Cosic. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I ask that you read the solemn declaration that the court usher has presented to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please be seated. Are you comfortable madam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You are now going to respond to questions put to you by Mr. Mikulicic, who is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Cosic.

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I hope you are accommodated properly. I am the Defence counsel for Mr. Aleksovski and I will ask you a few questions and ask you to answer them to the best of your recollection. Now, only for the record, Mrs. Cosic, will you please tell us your date and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: 12th of March, 1958.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Krcevine, Municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And where do you live?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: In Busovaca, that is the locality itself. In the environs, the village of Skradno.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You say you live in the village of Skradno, how far is it from the Town of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Two, I should say 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us something about your education?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I came from the secondary medical school, from nurse's school?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where did you attend that school?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: In Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Which stream?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: General medical stream.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When did you complete your education?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And after that you found a job?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I got the job at the health centre in Busocava in 1982.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you have been on this staff ever since?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You are still on their staff?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Cosic, what is your ethnic origin and are you a believer, if yes, what?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I am a Croat and a Roman Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said you lived in the village of Skradno, could you tell us something about the ethnic structure of the village of Skradno and I mean the time before the complete breakout in the Municipality of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: The ethnic structure, well, you could say that it was 50/50, 50 per cent Croats and 50 per cent Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the time when the conflict commenced in the village of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know when that was?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: On the 25th of January, '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Why has this date stuck in your memory, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: On the 25th of January, I worked, I was on duty there at the emergency. Therefore from seven o'clock in the morning until seven o'clock in the evening. And before the shift we were warned that our colleague who was to take over, could not come. That he could not come because something was going on. And that was how that began to consult with each other about what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And so what was happening?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: In the morning, my fellow knows, my colleague let me go home, saying that she would manage about the shift and I waited for some understanding because I had four children at home. And she had, who to look after her children, and a male colleague said that because of his personal safety he wouldn't dare, that the roads to Kacuni were closed and that all the passers by, all the workers, were coming back because the couldn't get through because there was fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Kacuni, do you know what was the ethnic structure of Kacuni at the time?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: The majority there were Muslims. There were also Croats, but Muslims constituted a majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, perhaps, if that day or perhaps the day before or the day after an incident took place in the village of Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, my colleague, therefore, remained on duty. And when it was decided when I would come next time when I (inaudible) obligation, she then told me that up there, a man of ours was killed and his name was Ivica Petrovic. And there was another young man with him, but I didn't remember his name. I forgot his name, whereas this one came from our village and that is why I remember what he wasn't called.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did your colleague first tell you how those two were killed, did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the details, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know how they were killed? Was it from firearms or from what he said?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: From her words, I gathered that somebody fired at them, that they were passing by in a car, what was a business or what errand, I wouldn't know, I don't know those particulars, but I think somebody fired at them. And after that as if they were harassed because there were also some knife wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And how large was the staff of the health centre, I mean the nurses and the medical personnel?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know exactly, but I think somewhere between 60 and 70, but I wouldn't know the exact figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How was the work organised in those shifts?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, we worked for 24 hours and then were for 48 hours off, three to four nurses, sometimes even five nurses, perhaps if one of us could simply put up with it, if we could manage it. It depended, of course, if necessity arose then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Cosic, do you remember that Busovaca was shelled at the same period of time?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us if you saw it, of course, or if you remember, where did these shells come from, where were they fired from?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: From the surroundings, I cannot remember exactly. I cannot remember, bring back this period of time. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But you say from the surroundings, you mean adjacent areas?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, adjacent areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us was it the slopes of the mountains around Busovaca or was it low lands?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I don't remember those details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Cosic, you said you took shifts and that one shift was 24 hours and that then you would have 48 hours off, did you go home to take a rest or did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I went home, I went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And how did you go home? Did you have some organised transport or did you walk there?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, each of us somehow managed by herself, but mostly on foot, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, the situation was too difficult, you could not organise the transport. So each one had to somehow manage by herself to see about how she would come to work and then go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was it dangerous?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes, it was dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Why was it dangerous?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, because of the shelling, because of the shelling. We never knew how we would fair. My colleague, a colleague of mine was wounded right in front of the health centre. She was leaving and I was coming to take over and nothing happened to me, but something happened to her and that is why we were afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Cosic, will you tell us, what were basically -- what kind of house services did the health centre offer, basically? Could you hospitalise your patients or was it only the primary care?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, we did our best to extend the most adequate care as possible, but it was just primary care by and large.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was there a room in the health centre, a room where you could accommodate a patient who needed rest, shall we say, or home care and things like that?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: We usually send people home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, I am asking you if there was a room within the health centre where they could perhaps lie down and stay under the medical control?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Oh, no, not on the premises of the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, if a patient was prescribed home care, it was because the health centre simply could not provide adequate accommodation for them, is it true?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Cosic, could you tell us, please, something about the supply, medical supply, medicines or other medical supplies, did you have enough of those?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: There were no shortages, the manager and the director and that the head nurse took care of this. We, the rest of us, of the paramedical medical staff did not observe any shortages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And generally speaking, something about the supplies, will you tell us, power supply, water supply, clothes, footwear, food?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: As for water supply, the water piping was damaged during the shelling on the 26th of April, 1992, so that we had to make do with certain things. And there were some shortages or whatever. We did have it and we didn't. By in large we did have enough water. And as for the electricity, there were power cuts and then we would be helped by UNPROFOR because they supplied us with power from their sources from their generating units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you cooperate with the UNPROFOR battalion in some other ways?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what kind of cooperation if you remember?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, they were helping us with the manager. They would receive, whenever something would crop up, about medicine or other necessities. So we were not all that informed, but we were simply wise to this cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned medicine, Ms. Cosic, was there a pharmacy in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: In the town, no, no, in the town, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you say in the town, no, but was there one working somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I mean within the health centre, yes, I cannot really remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. I understand, after all, it was six years ago.

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and I want to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Of course, Mrs. Cosic, that is what is expected of you. Mrs. Cosic, what was the structure, I mean the ethnic structure of patients treated at the health centre in Busovaca? Did this patient population include all the Croats and Muslims and Serbs or what was it during?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Do you mean during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I mean before and during.

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, ethnic structure, there were all Croats, Muslims, and Serbs before and after. Except that afterwards there were fewer. I mean fewer because this population had already left before the conflict. They were not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you say that the population left before the conflict, can you tell us something more about it, what do you know about it and how do you know it?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I know it because on the 24th and that was a day when I worked and prior to that, these people were getting ready and leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you please be more accurate, more definite when you say "these people," whom do you mean?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I mean the Muslim people. Inhabitants. A worker who worked on the 24th, I don't know her surname, I think her name was Senida, that was her first name, she used to say herself that their relatives, friends, neighbours, were going and she was talking to me and said, and I don't know why they're going. And I turned to her and said that I didn't know why they were leaving, I wasn't clear about that, about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you try to recall if it was before the 24th when you said that the conflict started or was it after that?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: No, it was before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Cosic, you also mentioned that even some of the employees of the health centre were of different ethnic origin, did you perhaps notice if the personnel of Muslim origin also left prior to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: In December already some of them were mentioning, some were talking about days in January about holidays, which baffled me slightly. And later on, of course, I understood some other facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was it that you understood subsequently, could you tell us, what facts?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Well, I realised that I perhaps knew that something was afoot, well about the conflict on the 25th. I mean when it broke out, then I simply related this with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Cosic, the interpreters ask you to speak a little slower if possible, so will you please slow down for the sake of proper interpretation. Mrs. Cosic, are you familiar with a place Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the facility, Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How do you know about them?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I live near Kaonik. It used to be the barracks of the former Yugoslav Peoples Army. And afterwards it was a prison, something, a prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Cosic, do you remember, when was it that the JNA left the barracks?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But would you know the year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was it the former or the latter half?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I think it was the former half.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Cosic, could you tell us, when was it that you met for the first time, patients coming from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Could you please be more clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, you were a nurse in the health centre in Busovaca and you treated, you extended medical help to patients who came to your room. When was it that you helped, the first time, the patients who were brought from Kaonik? When did it start?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: It started in -- it was in early February.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Cosic, do you know who brought those patients from Kaonik to the health centre in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Zlatko Aleksovski, director.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When did you meet Mr. Aleksovski for the first time?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: I met him then, when he brought prisoners from the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said it was sometime in early February '92. Did you have an opportunity to talk to Mr. Aleksovski on various occasions?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you recognise him if you saw him today?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Cosic, would you then look around the courtroom and tell us if you see Mr. Aleksovski in it. Sorry. Could you tell us where Mr. Aleksovski is sitting?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Behind you

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, please, Mr. Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said Mr. Aleksovski used to bring patients from the Kaonik facility. Was he alone or did somebody else bring them in?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA STAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, but Zlatko brought them as a rule. And he would also bring them escorted by guards.
